title: Bedrock Rockhound Flip-Flop Sandal Review – Spencer Harding
content:
While Spencer‘s disdain for flip-flops initially led him toward Bedrock Sandal‘s sportier sandal offerings, he couldn’t resist his curiosity when Bedrock announced their Rockhound flip-flop. Could Bedrock’s version of a flip-flop sway his lifelong aversion to the footwear? Read his review below…

You’ll rarely find someone who is more of a Bedrock sandal evangelist than I am. After spending a decade in Chacos before their demise at the hands of venture capital under Wolverine, I found myself looking for a proper pair of adventure sandals. I was living in the Bay Area where Bedrock Sandals was founded and located at the time. Dan, one of the founders of Bedrock, kicked off his Cairns toward me as I was about to head off for the Baja Divide Grand Depart back in 2016. I wore those sandals for years and have been a devout Bedrock evangelist ever since. I describe my Cairns as “the greatest piece of footwear I have ever owned.”

Now, almost every time I have done a hike or bike or whatever in my sandals, some man will yell, “Look, honey, he’s doing this in flip-flops.” When I guided in Zion NPS and hiked Angel’s Landing weekly, this would happen far too often. Vying for dad superiority, I would look them in the eyes and say, “These are sports sandals, boss, check the heel strap.” In the above photo, where I’m covered in glacial silt, one of my fellow hikers looked at my feet with concern as we navigated a steep moraine to get to an ice cave. He asked if I normally hiked like this in my sandals. As I reminisced about hiking into the Grand Canyon the hardest way possible in my Cairns, I just said, “Yeah,” as my friend Tyler, who was on that trip, laughed.

Even growing up in Southern California, I’ve always had a disdain for flip-flops. I never enjoyed the loose fit and constant thwacking of the soles on my feet. It felt like walking around with your shoelaces untied. I can see their merit as a house shoe or very casual footwear, but can there be an adventure flip-flop? I’d argue no, but there is merit in having a high-quality flip-flop if you are not as averse to the concept as me…

Bedrock Rockhound Quick Hits

  • Grippy + Durable Vibram® XS Trek EVO rubber compound
  • Cushioned 3D+ EVA Footbed
  • Upper: Premium polyester and nylon webbing
  • Strap System: Bedrock’s patent-pending Rockhound G-Hook adjustment system
  • Made in South Korea
  • Max Cushioning: 16 mm (19 mm for Nubuck version)
  • Sizes: 5-14
  • Available in black, slate blue, and Nubuck Leather
  • $90 for standard and $130 for Nubuck Leather

A New Flip Flop, Same Quality Materials

It would be easy to expect that Bedrock might just eliminate the heel strap on their Cairn and poof, flip-flop, but that’s not what happened here. Bedrock re-used their softer C footbed compound in the Rockhound with the slimmer 16 mm footbed thickness of the Cairn.

The straps have been redesigned for Rockhound, but the adjustability of the bomber hook-and-loop closure will feel familiar. To protect people’s feet, Bedrock have introduced a small piece of webbing to shield the skin between toes from the paracord that connects the straps to the sole.

The 3D+ footbed is their most supportive arch yet and, as with all Bedrock footwear, the Rockhound sports a high-quality Vibram rubber outsole. Like the rest of their stock, the Rockhound can be re-soled at their Montana headquarters.

How Does the Rockhound Compare?

The first thing that caught my attention was the softer C-compound footbed found in Bedrock’s thicker C-series sandals. Having spent so much time in the standard Cairn and not the thicker C-series sandals, I found the softer compound more alien than I expected. I have a well-seasoned piece of skin between my two biggest toes, so I looked with disdain at the extra webbing intended to smooth out the feeling of the paracord. I have never personally had an issue with the paracord or the softness of the soles in my Bedrocks, and this triggered a larger question: had Bedrock lost the plot? Was the Rockhound a dilution of their ideals for the larger market?

I don’t believe Bedrock has lost the plot, but with new footwear, they do need to iterate and bring a wider awareness to their brand and what they offer. If Bedrock had never progressed past their initial very minimal sandals, they would never have made the Cairn. While there is probably an overlap between the sport sandal and flip-flop market, there is good reason why people want the convenience of a flip-flop over a heel strap. I see people constantly wandering around in their Cairns with the heel strap crushed under their heel. There are, of course, going to be people who don’t want to spend years training their feet to be okay with hard soles and cordage between their toes. A chief complaint I hear when I recommend the Cairn is friends’ woes about having anything between their toes. I think I would have, on a surface level, appreciated the Rockhound as a more faithful adaptation of Bedrock’s previous sandals without the cordage cover and squishy sole.

I’m not here to totally be a Bedrock Sandal curmudgeon; the Rockhound is a quality sandal indeed. While I will almost always reach for my Cairns over the Rockhound sandals, they are a very high-quality flip-flop in a market where most iterations feel disposable. The Nubuck leather version conjures up memories of the cult-like following of Rainbow Sandals, of which the Rockhound feels a spiritual successor.

The Rockhounds weren’t enough to convince me to be a dedicated flip-flopper, but if you are already a flip-flop aficionado and looking for a quality pair of sandals made with the best rubber that can be resoled time and time again, then the Rockhound might just be for you.

Pros

  • Vibram soles are grippy and resoleable at Bedrock’s Montana HQ
  • Sizing was true to other shoes and previous Bedrock Sandals
  • Softer C compound for more cushion
  • Protective webbing over cordage between toes
  • Contoured 3D+ footbed provides plenty of arch support

Cons

  • I would have preferred the traditional harder footbed compound
  • I still don’t really like flip-flops over a heel strap
